extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, criminologists, cultural/cinematic studies researchers, and policymakers interested in corporate harms and the opioid epidemic
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis that uses horror-genre tropes to theorize, describe, and critique the character and legal treatment of corporate harms (exemplified by Purdue/OxyContin and The Fall of the House of Usher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depersonalization of victims / exclusion from screen
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims are frequently excluded, unnamed, or non-speaking and therefore presented as an unidentifiable mass, which reduces emotional resonance and audience empathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in The House of Usher the victims of the opioid epidemic are off screen (except for one), and mass deaths (e.g., hundreds burned under acid) produce unrecognisable victims; this excess of unknown victims 'contaminates' audience capacity to care. Anti-pattern: focusing spectacle on mass harm without depicting individual sufferings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fates worse than death as a descriptive framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror’s vocabulary of imaginative, non-bloody harms (e.g., living death, removal from one’s life) is especially useful to capture the kinds of harms corporate wrongdoing inflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guided by genre examples (vampires, zombies, Weeping Angels), the paper aligns addiction with 'living death'—loss of agency and personhood—arguing such tropes illuminate harms that legal categories may not capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of personhood / loss of agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms that remove individuals from their lives, relationships, or selfhood (e.g., being buried alive, time-displaced, or consumed by addiction) are especially horrific and apt analogies for addiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Poe’s entombment, Doctor Who’s Weeping Angels, and OxyContin addiction which 'rob[s] a person of who they are'. Use these to emphasize the qualitative nature of harm beyond mortality statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms assessed by impact on relationships and moral dilemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure of horror (and corporate harm) is how it degrades interpersonal bonds and forces loved ones into soul-destroying moral grey zones (e.g., deciding whether to evict or support an addicted family member).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative examples (zombie-family dilemmas, choices around addicted loved ones) to show interpersonal consequences; note that this stresses social/relational harms rather than individual pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schema incongruence for criminal law
rubrics_metrics.description: Many corporate harms exceed or do not fit existing criminal-law categories because of scale, corporate form, time/proximity, and who counts as a criminal legal subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text argues OxyContin harms are 'schema incongruent'—harmful and blameworthy yet not adequately captured by criminal categories; implication: legal categories need revision to encompass corporate-scale harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine horror: banal/ everyday mode of inflicting harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms inflicted through ordinary, routine, and banal activities (prescribing for everyday pain, common products) produce a distinctive horror because they render the mundane dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: OxyContin prescribed for routine pain; parallels with slasher tropes that make gardening, sleeping, or drinking water sites of danger. Highlight how routinization normalizes harm and obscures culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complicity and banal participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine nature of corporate harms creates complicity among ordinary actors (family members, doctors, patients) who participate innocently or unwittingly in harm production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include loved ones requesting pain relief, doctors prescribing under misleading information, and patients demanding the drug; use to foreground hermeneutic harms of guilt and social contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of authority as an enabling trope
rubrics_metrics.description: A core dimension is the betrayal and collapse of institutions (regulators, scientific research, medical profession, law) that are supposed to protect the public, enabling corporate harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use horror tropes where institutions fail (Jaws, Poltergeist, Resident Evil) as analogues; emphasize effects on public trust and the 'destabilizing' horror of institutional betrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation and misuse of scientific methods and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations can manufacture, select, or misuse 'evidence' (e.g., limited letters vs peer-reviewed research) to create a veneer of legitimacy for harmful products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Purdue cited weak or company-funded studies and engaged in data selection and presentation; this is framed as a failure of scientific methods when overcome by corporate misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blaming victims / hermeneutic injustice (gaslighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate narratives that individualize blame (e.g., 'misuse', 'pseudo-addiction') constitute a form of hermeneutic injustice, gaslighting victims and obscuring corporate responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purdue's creation of 'pseudo-addiction' and calls to increase dosage are cited as instances; treat such narratives as both analytically and morally salient when assessing corporate harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory capture and specific regulatory failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory agencies (example: the FDA) failed in pre-market approval (accepting 'very rare' addiction claims without robust evidence) and in post-market surveillance and enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete regulatory failures—label approval, slow relabeling, close industry ties—to assess how regulatory malfunctioned; consider institutional incentives and oversight gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical profession capture and perverse incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture of medical professionals via incentives, 'key opinion leaders', and salesforces that misrepresent safety and push higher dosages is a distinct criterion for culpability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include financial incentives to prescribers and aggressive sales reps; evaluate the contamination of medical trust and its role in scaling harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal process as additional victim harm (Kafkaesque litigation/settlement dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing legal remedies and procedures can themselves extend victims’ suffering—through protracted processes, inadequate deterrence, and settlements that shield corporate actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bankruptcy-based settlements that limit accountability, protracted MDL processes, and releases of individual family members from liability; consider whether remedies functionally deter repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate phoenixing and evasion of accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate tactics (rebranding, bankruptcy, shielding owners via corporate veil) that allow entities or individuals to escape meaningful accountability are a criterion for evaluating systemic failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Purdue emerging as 'Knoa Therapeutics' post-bankruptcy and Sackler family retaining wealth; policy implication: need for reforms addressing phoenixing and veil-piercing to ensure redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuit of profit as an organizing motive and normalizing harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The profit-seeking logic of corporations, including cost–benefit analyses that accept human harm as a cost of business, is central to how harms are produced and normalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical sales/profit data (OxyContin revenue growth) and theoretical claims (Friedman, Bakan) to show the moral disgust of monetized harm; evaluate corporate structure and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative focus on individual spectacle vs structural culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural narratives often individualize blame and dramatize individual fates (e.g., family members) rather than tracing responsibility to the board/ corporation, which obscures structural culpability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The House of Usher focuses on family individuals while 'the Board' remains unseen; use this to critique representational choices that hinder legal/structural accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror genre as a tool for redescription and mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Using horror tropes provides conceptual language and emotional registers that can make visible the scope and intensity of corporate wrongdoing and provoke public or legal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors propose horror offers frameworks lacking in law to express these harms and to motivate responses (disgust, transgression); implication: interdisciplinary narrative strategies can supplement legal reform efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for criminal law and regulatory reform to capture corporate harms
rubrics_metrics.description: A prescriptive criterion: criminal categories and regulatory mechanisms must be adapted so corporations can be punished as criminal legal subjects and so corporate-scale harms are no longer 'schema incongruent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues for changing criminal law categories and regulatory mechanisms (e.g., addressing corporate veil, enforcement practices) so that legal norms reflect the scale and character of corporate harms.
